To Race or Not to Race? Exploiting Performance Variability in Mixed-Integer Programming via Root-Gated Resource Allocation

Mourchid Adegbindin    Brenda Dietrich    Jamol Pender Affiliation: Department of Operations Research and Information Engineering
Cornell University, Ithaca, NY, USA, 14853 E-mail ma757@cornell.edu, bld34@cornell.edu, jjp274@cornell.edu
Abstract

Mixed-integer programming (MIP) solver runtimes vary substantially across random seeds. Parallel replication exploits this variability but can waste computational resources when applied indiscriminately. We investigate whether information from an ordinary solve can guide this allocation decision.

We formulate replication under a finite deadline, establish an exact relationship between runtime dispersion and the value of independent searches, and analyze delayed replication and imperfect allocation decisions. Using 101,615 seeded SCIP runs, we examine the association between root-LP dual degeneracy and replication value. We then introduce a non-invasive root-gated policy that preserves the original solver trajectory and launches three additional seeded processes when a root dual-degeneracy indicator reaches a fixed threshold.

In a prospective two-hour experiment on 130 paired instances, root-gated racing proves optimality on 77 instances (59.23%), versus 73 (56.15%) for both Single and unconditional Race-4, while reducing active worker-process occupancy by 43.00% relative to unconditional racing. These findings demonstrate the promise of selective parallel resource allocation without solver-source modifications.

Keywords: 
mixed-integer programming performance variability dual degeneracy resource allocation.

1 Introduction

Mixed-integer programming (MIP) is an essential tool for planning, scheduling, and resource allocation. In many applications, an optimization run must deliver a solution within a prescribed time window under a limited computational budget. The usefulness of the resulting decision depends directly on the reliability of that computation.

Yet modern MIP solvers exhibit substantial runtime variability across random seeds: identical models, settings, and hardware can yield markedly different branch-and-bound trajectories, with one run proving optimality while another reaches the time limit. This unpredictability complicates resource planning: insufficient capacity risks missed deadlines, while excessive allocation wastes computation.

Independent seeded searches can improve the chance of a timely proof, but consume additional processor time, memory, and computing capacity, often without benefit on less seed-sensitive instances. The central question is therefore: When does information available during an ongoing MIP solve justify allocating additional processors to alternative search trajectories? We address this decision under a finite deadline, accounting explicitly for wall-clock time and aggregate computational effort.

1.1 Approach and Related Work

Performance variability in MIP is well documented [5, 13, 14, 9]. Adegbindin et al. [1] quantify this variability across randomized SCIP runs and examine its relationship with instance structure and early solver information. Their work establishes that performance variability is not merely experimental noise, but a measurable feature of MIP computation with potential operational consequences.

The exploitation of variability through randomized search is well established. Algorithm portfolios exploit performance differences across alternative strategies [11]. Fischetti and Monaci [7] develop a bet-and-run approach that conducts short randomized searches and selects a promising trajectory for continuation. Fischetti et al. [6] investigate randomized sampling in branch-and-cut, including information collected from diversified root searches. Carvajal et al. [4] study parallel branch-and-bound trees that exchange information during execution. Commercial solvers also support concurrent MIP optimization through independent searches [12].

Other methods use information collected during execution to intervene in the search itself. Anderson et al. [3] use online estimates of remaining branch-and-bound tree size to guide restart decisions. Adegbindin et al. [2] develop an LP-state steering framework that modifies the state inherited by branch-and-bound. These approaches demonstrate the value of intervening in an ongoing computation, but address different control decisions.

Our work addresses a complementary question. Rather than modifying the search trajectory, we ask whether information produced by an ordinary solve can determine when additional search trajectories are worth their computational cost. One solver process begins normally, and the controller observes its first solved root linear program (LP). At this checkpoint, the controller decides whether to continue with the original process alone or allocate additional processors to independent seeded searches. The original trajectory is preserved in either case.

The decision relies on a simple dual-degeneracy statistic: the fraction of eligible nonbasic LP columns with zero or near-zero reduced cost. Gamrath, Berthold, and Salvagnin [8] study this classical degeneracy measure; we investigate its value as an early resource-allocation signal. A fixed threshold determines whether three additional seeded processes launch. The controller operates through SCIP’s existing interface and standard operating-system process controls, without modifying solver source code or exchanging information between replicas.

This design creates a tradeoff absent from immediate replication. Additional processes start only after the root LP becomes available, and their computational cost must be justified against the remaining deadline. We analyze this tradeoff through the distributional value of independent replication, delayed launches, and imperfect allocation decisions.

Contributions. We make three contributions. First, we develop a finite-deadline analysis of randomized replication, with explicit accounting for delayed launches, processor consumption, and imperfect allocation decisions. Second, using 101,615 seeded SCIP runs, we examine whether root-LP dual degeneracy identifies instances for which additional search trajectories have value, and quantify the opportunities captured and missed by a fixed threshold. Third, we implement a solver-external controller that preserves the original trajectory while selectively launching independent seeded searches. On 130 prospectively paired instances at a two-hour deadline, Root-Gated proves optimality on 77 instances, against 73 for both single-seed solving and unconditional Race-4, while reducing active worker occupancy by 43.00% relative to Race-4.

2 When Does Racing Pay?

2.1 Replication and Computational Cost

2.2 Delayed Replication under a Finite Deadline

A baseline solver process starts at time zero and reaches its first solved root LP at elapsed time a<Ta<T. The remaining wall-clock budget is b=T−ab=T-a. The analysis is conditional on reaching this checkpoint before the deadline. If no valid root observation becomes available, the implemented policy continues the baseline process without diversification.

At the checkpoint, the controller chooses between continuing the baseline alone and launching m−1m-1 additional seeded processes, where m≥2m\geq 2. Let RR denote the remaining time to proof for the baseline process in isolation. Let X1,…,Xm−1X_{1},\ldots,X_{m-1} denote the completion times of the alternative processes, measured from their effective start times, and put Y=min1≤i≤m−1⁡XiY=\min_{1\leq i\leq m-1}X_{i}.

The additional processes become active after a common, fixed delay hh, where 0≤h<b0\leq h<b. Let H≥0H\geq 0 denote additional processor-equivalent work incurred during launch, monitoring, and termination that is not included in the active-replica consumption below. We assume 𝔼⁡[H]<∞\mathbb{E}[H]<\infty.

Assuming that diversification does not alter the baseline trajectory, the remaining elapsed times under continuation and diversification are

W0=min⁡{R,b},W1=min⁡{R,h+Y,b}.W_{0}=\min\{R,b\},\qquad W_{1}=\min\{R,h+Y,b\}. (4)

We evaluate both actions using processor-slot consumption, a wall-clock weight λ≥0\lambda\geq 0, and a penalty P>0P>0 for failure to prove optimality by the deadline. The remaining cost of continuation is

J0=(1+λ)W0+P𝟏{R>b}.J_{0}=(1+\lambda)W_{0}+P\mathbf{1}_{\{R>b\}}. (5)

Δ:=J1−J0=(1+λ)​(W1−W0)+(m−1)​(W1−h)++H−P𝟏{R>b,h+Y≤b}.\boxed{\begin{aligned} \Delta:=J_{1}-J_{0}={}&(1+\lambda)(W_{1}-W_{0})\\ &+(m-1)(W_{1}-h)_{+}+H\\ &-P\mathbf{1}_{\{R>b,\ h+Y\leq b\}}.\end{aligned}} (7)

Let ℐ\mathcal{I} denote the information available at the checkpoint, including aa and the fixed model parameter hh. Define

S0​(t)=Pr⁡(R>t∣ℐ),S_{0}(t)=\Pr(R>t\mid\mathcal{I}),

S1(t)=Pr(R>t,h+Y>t∣ℐ).S_{1}(t)=\Pr(R>t,\ h+Y>t\mid\mathcal{I}).

Proposition 1 (Conditional value of delayed replication)

Under the preceding assumptions,

𝔼⁡[Δ∣ℐ]=𝔼⁡[H∣ℐ]+(m−1)∫hbS1(t)dt−(1+λ)∫hb[S0(t)−S1(t)]dt−P⁡[S0​(b)−S1​(b)].\boxed{\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[\Delta\mid\mathcal{I}]={}&\mathbb{E}[H\mid\mathcal{I}]\\ &+(m-1)\int_{h}^{b}S_{1}(t)\,dt\\ &-(1+\lambda)\int_{h}^{b}[S_{0}(t)-S_{1}(t)]\,dt\\ &-P[S_{0}(b)-S_{1}(b)].\end{aligned}} (8)

The proof is given in Appendix 0.A. Diversification has lower conditional expected cost precisely when 𝔼⁡[Δ∣ℐ]<0\mathbb{E}[\Delta\mid\mathcal{I}]<0.

The model assumes simultaneous activation of the additional replicas and continuous activity until the race terminates. The implementation permits staggered starts and individual worker termination; its resource consumption is measured from observed process lifetimes. Moreover, active worker occupancy differs from capacity reserved by a fixed-size batch allocation.

2.3 Allocation Decisions with an Imperfect Signal

Let G∈{0,1}G\in\{0,1\} be an ℐ\mathcal{I}-measurable decision rule, where G=1G=1 indicates diversification. Its realized cost is JG=J0+G​ΔJ_{G}=J_{0}+G\Delta. Consequently,

𝔼⁡[JG]<𝔼⁡[J0]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[J_{G}]<\mathbb{E}[J_{0}] ⇔𝔼⁡[G​Δ]<0,\displaystyle\iff\mathbb{E}[G\Delta]<0, (9)
𝔼⁡[JG]<𝔼⁡[J1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[J_{G}]<\mathbb{E}[J_{1}] ⇔𝔼⁡[(1−G)​Δ]>0.\displaystyle\iff\mathbb{E}[(1-G)\Delta]>0.

Let δ⁡(ℐ)=𝔼⁡[Δ∣ℐ]\delta(\mathcal{I})=\mathbb{E}[\Delta\mid\mathcal{I}] and define the optimal checkpoint rule

G⋆=𝟏{δ(ℐ)<0}.G^{\star}=\mathbf{1}_{\{\delta(\mathcal{I})<0\}}.
Proposition 2 (Cost of an imperfect allocation signal)

For every ℐ\mathcal{I}-measurable binary gate GG,

𝔼[JG]−𝔼[JG⋆]=𝔼[|δ(ℐ)|𝟏{G≠G⋆}].\boxed{\mathbb{E}[J_{G}]-\mathbb{E}[J_{G^{\star}}]=\mathbb{E}\left[|\delta(\mathcal{I})|\mathbf{1}_{\{G\neq G^{\star}\}}\right].} (10)

The proof is given in Appendix 0.A. The regret from an allocation error depends on its expected cost, rather than its frequency alone.

For comparison, let BqB_{q} be a binary random decision independent of (J0,J1,G)(J_{0},J_{1},G), with Pr⁡(Bq=1)=q=𝔼⁡[G]\Pr(B_{q}=1)=q=\mathbb{E}[G]. Then

The optimal rule G⋆G^{\star} depends on conditional runtime and cost distributions unavailable for a new instance. We therefore restrict attention to an inexpensive structural statistic obtained during the baseline solve. The resulting threshold policy approximates the conditional cost decision; its effectiveness depends on the association between the statistic and the marginal value of replication. Section  3 examines this association using historical solver runs.

2.4 The Time-Zero Racing Benchmark

Let X0=a+RX_{0}=a+R denote the baseline trajectory’s total completion time, conditional on reaching the checkpoint, and let YY denote the alternative portfolio’s completion time under the same isolated seeded trajectories. Under a coupling that preserves these trajectories across policies, immediate time-zero racing has completion time

Drace0=min⁡{X0,Y}.D_{\mathrm{race0}}=\min\{X_{0},Y\}.

For a root-gated policy,

DG={X0,G=0,min⁡{X0,a+h+Y},G=1.D_{G}=\begin{cases}X_{0},&G=0,\\ \min\{X_{0},a+h+Y\},&G=1.\end{cases} (12)

Since a+h≥0a+h\geq 0,

Drace0≤DGalmost surely.D_{\mathrm{race0}}\leq D_{G}\qquad\text{almost surely}. (13)

Thus, under this coupling, immediate racing provides a lower bound on completion time and an upper bound on deadline proof probability for root-gated racing. This ordering need not hold when concurrent execution alters the individual solver trajectories through resource contention or other interactions.

The resource-allocation objective is to recover useful deadline protection while reducing unnecessary parallel computation. The implemented decision rule is

G=𝟏{droot≥d⋆},G=\mathbf{1}_{\{d_{\mathrm{root}}\geq d^{\star}\}}, (14)

when a valid root statistic is available, and G=0G=0 otherwise. Here drootd_{\mathrm{root}} is the root dual-degeneracy indicator and d⋆d^{\star} is a fixed threshold. Its effectiveness is evaluated empirically, rather than assumed from the replication theory.

3 When Does Variability Become Actionable?

3.1 The Seeded-Run Corpus

We examine 101,615 seeded SCIP runs covering 1,017 distinct instances from the MIPLIB 2017 collection [10], under a nominal four-hour time limit. Of these, 1,016 instances have 100 recorded runs and one has 15. The records contain terminal statuses, solving times, random seeds, branch-and-bound statistics, and early solver measurements.

Among these runs, 42,877 terminate optimally, 56,452 reach the time limit, 1,704 have other statuses, and 582 lack parsed status. First-LP basis and reduced-cost counts are available for 92,548 runs, with a defined root-degeneracy ratio in 92,048. Appendix 0.B provides the full audit.

We count an optimality proof only when the recorded status is optimal and its completion time does not exceed deadline TT; time-limited runs are right-censored. The Weighted Variability Score (WVS) of [1] describes cross-seed variability but is not an input to the online allocation policy.

3.2 Empirical Value of Replication

We first isolate the value of replication independently of any root-based decision rule. For each instance, we form disjoint blocks of four recorded seeds: one baseline and three alternative trajectories. An ideal four-seed race proves optimality by deadline TT whenever at least one seed does. Its completion time is the minimum of the four trajectories, capped at TT. This time-zero counterfactual excludes launch delays, overhead, and hardware contention.

The audit yields 24,798 eligible blocks from 994 instances. At four hours, ideal Race-4 increases proof probability from 43.04% to 45.67%, recovering 654 additional proofs. Among 113 retrospectively identified mixed-outcome instances, the 2,818 eligible blocks yield 47.48% and 70.69%, respectively: a 23.21 percentage-point gain. At 15 minutes, the corresponding all-block fractions are 31.08% and 33.51%.

This reliability gain carries substantial cost: mean ideal processor consumption rises from 2.44 to 9.35 processor-hours per block. The historical proof curves appear in Appendix 0.B. Thus, replication creates valuable proof opportunities, but unconditional deployment expends substantial resources on instances with little additional benefit.

3.3 Root Dual-Degeneracy Indicator

We investigate whether the first solved root LP identifies valuable replication opportunities. Our signal is the classical dual-degeneracy rate [8]. Let 𝒩\mathcal{N} denote eligible nonbasic LP columns and c¯j\bar{c}_{j} their reduced costs. For numerical tolerance εrc\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rc}}, define

droot=|{j∈𝒩:|c¯j|≤εrc}||𝒩|.d_{\mathrm{root}}=\frac{\left|\left\{j\in\mathcal{N}:|\bar{c}_{j}|\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rc}}\right\}\right|}{|\mathcal{N}|}. (15)

The historical records yield the proxy

d^root=Nnonbasic,zeroRCNcolumns−Nbasic.\widehat{d}_{\mathrm{root}}=\frac{N_{\mathrm{nonbasic,zeroRC}}}{N_{\mathrm{columns}}-N_{\mathrm{basic}}}. (16)

Records with missing counts or nonpositive denominators remain undefined, never zero. Both measurements use nonbasic statuses lower, upper, or zero and reduced-cost tolerance 10−610^{-6}. The historical proxy reconstructs logged basis counts, whereas the prospective controller examines eligible LP columns directly; exact equivalence is unverified. The threshold d⋆=0.25d^{\star}=0.25 was fixed heuristically, without calibration on the historical corpus.

3.4 Does Root Degeneracy Identify Valuable Races?

We associate each baseline root statistic with the subsequent outcomes of its four seeded trajectories. Let Qi​b(1)Q_{ib}^{(1)} and Qi​b(4)Q_{ib}^{(4)} indicate optimality proofs by deadline for the baseline and ideal race. The incremental proof benefit is

Bi​b=Qi​b(4)−Qi​b(1).B_{ib}=Q_{ib}^{(4)}-Q_{ib}^{(1)}. (17)

Here Bi​b=1B_{ib}=1 identifies a proof obtained by an alternative seed but missed by the baseline.

Of the 24,798 eligible blocks, 22,963 from 930 instances have a defined baseline root ratio. The fixed threshold d⋆=0.25d^{\star}=0.25 activates on 11,574 of these blocks (50.40%) and identifies 459 of the 654 additional-proof opportunities (70.18%). The remaining 195 opportunities lie below threshold; none occur among blocks with unavailable root measurements.

On the root-observed subset, Single proves 44.22% of blocks and unconditional ideal Race-4 proves 47.07%. Selective time-zero racing achieves 46.22% with 5.77 processor-hours per block, versus 9.18 for Race-4: a 37.15% reduction. Independent random activation at the same 50.40% rate yields an expected proof fraction of 45.65% and 5.82 processor-hours.

Figure 1 shows that the association is nonmonotone: low root degeneracy does not preclude seed sensitivity, nor does high degeneracy guarantee beneficial replication. Nevertheless, the fixed threshold concentrates 70.18% of observed proof opportunities within approximately half the eligible blocks.

These historical comparisons establish the potential value of selective replication, not the performance of its delayed implementation. Section 5 evaluates the executable policy prospectively.

4 Root-Gated Resource Allocation

4.1 Root Diversification Gate

We implement the allocation decision of Section 2 using the root dual-degeneracy indicator of Section 3.3. One SCIP process begins normally; after its first solved root LP, the controller makes a single allocation decision. For a fixed threshold d⋆=0.25d^{\star}=0.25, the rule is

G⁡(droot)={0,droot<d⋆,1,droot≥d⋆,G(d_{\mathrm{root}})=\begin{cases}0,&d_{\mathrm{root}}<d^{\star},\\ 1,&d_{\mathrm{root}}\geq d^{\star},\end{cases} (18)

where G=0G=0 retains the original process alone and G=1G=1 launches three additional seeded searches. Invalid or unavailable root observations, or a completed baseline solve, trigger no replicas. The original trajectory continues undisturbed in either case. The threshold was fixed heuristically before the prospective evaluation, not calibrated on a separate discovery set.

4.2 Solver-External Implementation and Asynchronous Launch

A PySCIPOpt handler captures the FIRSTLPSOLVED event at the root node. For an optimal root LP, it computes drootd_{\mathrm{root}} from eligible nonbasic columns with reduced-cost magnitude at most 10−610^{-6}. An atomic JSON record exposes the statistic, its counts, and validity to an external Python controller. Neither SCIP source code nor the active search algorithms are modified.

The maximum portfolio size is m=4m=4, with seeds assigned by

sb​k=sbase+4b+k,k=0,1,2,3.s_{bk}=s_{\mathrm{base}}+4b+k,\qquad k=0,1,2,3. (19)

All comparison policies use the same seed block. Unlike unconditional Race-4, which starts all four processes immediately, Root-Gated launches replicas asynchronously after the root observation. Each receives only the remaining global time budget; replicas exchange no search information. The complete controller appears in Algorithm 1 of Appendix 0.B.

4.3 Termination and Outcome Accounting

The controller evaluates terminal certificates against the common global deadline using recorded monotonic completion timestamps. Optimality proofs constitute the primary endpoint; infeasibility certificates are recorded separately, and missing terminal records never count as proofs. Upon recognizing a certificate, the controller terminates the remaining workers. Otherwise, processes may continue until their individual solver time limits expire. Thus, the proof deadline governs outcome classification, whereas resource accounting reflects the observed lifetime of each worker.

For controller-recorded worker launch and stopping times sk,eks_{k},e_{k}, aggregate worker-process occupancy under policy π\pi is

Cπslot=∑k∈ℒπ(ek−sk),C_{\pi}^{\mathrm{slot}}=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{L}_{\pi}}(e_{k}-s_{k}), (20)

where ℒπ\mathcal{L}_{\pi} is the set of launched workers. This measure captures aggregate process occupancy rather than CPU utilization or scheduler-reserved capacity.

5 Computational Evaluation

We evaluate whether root information supports selective parallel execution under a common deadline. Unlike the historical time-zero comparisons, these experiments execute the three policies prospectively on the cluster.

5.1 Experimental Design

We use 130 preselected MIPLIB 2017 instances, with one paired four-seed block per instance (1001-1004). All 390 portfolio trials form complete, deadline-matched triples at T=7200T=7200 seconds. The threshold d⋆=0.25d^{\star}=0.25 was fixed heuristically before execution, without calibration on the historical corpus. An earlier 50-instance run served only as an engineering shakedown.

Experiments ran through PySCIPOpt 5.4.1 on Seneca’s cac_cpu partition. Each SCIP worker was intended to use one core; parallel portfolios reserved four Slurm CPUs, even when the gate remained closed. All policies used the same seed block, but their separate executions could experience different runtime conditions. We assess uncertainty through 12,000 paired bootstrap resamples of the 130 instances.

5.2 Policies and Performance Measures

Single executes the baseline seed; Race-4 launches all four seeds immediately; Root-Gated launches three additional seeds only when a valid root measurement reaches d⋆d^{\star}. All processes share the original deadline.

Let QiπQ_{i}^{\pi} indicate an optimality proof by the deadline for policy π\pi on instance ii. We estimate proof probability and mean worker occupancy by

p^π=1n​∑i=1nQiπ,c^π=1n​∑i=1nCπ,islot,n=130.\widehat{p}_{\pi}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}Q_{i}^{\pi},\qquad\widehat{c}_{\pi}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}C_{\pi,i}^{\mathrm{slot}},\qquad n=130. (21)

The relative occupancy saving is

CostSaving=1−c^Gatec^Race4.\mathrm{CostSaving}=1-\frac{\widehat{c}_{\mathrm{Gate}}}{\widehat{c}_{\mathrm{Race4}}}. (22)

Worker occupancy sums active process lifetimes; portfolio wall time includes controller cleanup. Neither quantity measures actual CPU utilization or Slurm-reserved capacity.

5.3 Main Computational Results

Root-Gated proves optimality on 77 of 130 instances, compared with 73 for both Single and Race-4. Its paired proof advantage is 3.08 percentage points over either comparator. The gain rests on four favorable paired discordances and no unfavorable ones; the exact two-sided McNemar test yields p=0.125p=0.125. Thus, the observed improvement is promising but does not establish statistical superiority under this exact test.

The resource difference is substantial. Root-Gated reduces mean active worker occupancy from 14891.91 to 8487.73 seconds per instance: a 43.00% saving (95% bootstrap interval: 34.51-51.39%), or 6404.18 seconds per trial. Mean wall time also falls by 225.39 seconds relative to Race-4 (95% interval: 117.94-350.37 seconds saved).

Active occupancy savings do not translate directly into reserved cluster capacity. Both parallel policies reserve four Slurm CPUs throughout their portfolio jobs. Multiplying mean wall time by four gives reservation proxies of 14898.84 and 13997.28 CPU-slot seconds for Race-4 and Root-Gated, respectively: only 6.05% savings. Realizing the larger active-occupancy benefit requires dynamic reallocation of otherwise idle cores.

5.4 The Value of the Root Gate

Root-Gated launches four workers on 70 of 130 instances (53.85%) and retains one on 60. Of 124 defined root ratios, 70 meet the threshold and 54 fall below it; six are unavailable. All gate decisions follow this classification.

For the 54 below-threshold instances, mean worker occupancy is 3844.81 seconds versus 17200.91 for Race-4. Above threshold, the respective means are 12487.61 and 13147.61 seconds. The gate thus concentrates resource savings among instances without diversification, although these comparisons do not establish the root statistic’s predictive value.

5.5 Heterogeneity and Failure Cases

Five instances have discordant proof outcomes; the other 125 agree across policies. Root-Gated proves four instances missed by each comparator, but two of its additional proofs relative to Single and three relative to Race-4 occur with the gate closed.

The gate decisions and paired proof-outcome patterns are detailed in Figure 4 of Appendix 0.B.

At fhnw-binpack4-48.mps, Root-Gated activates and succeeds where both comparators fail. At k1mushroomi.mps, it alone succeeds despite a closed gate. These outcomes expose execution variability rather than an isolated causal effect of the threshold. A prospective random-gate comparator was not executed; repeated seed blocks and resource-matched controls remain necessary to assess the signal’s predictive contribution.

6 Discussion and Practical Implications

Performance variability is usually treated as a source of computational uncertainty to be measured or mitigated. Our results suggest a complementary perspective: variability creates opportunities for selective resource allocation. Rather than commit four processors before search begins, a solver can use information from its first solved root LP to decide whether additional trajectories warrant their cost.

The prospective experiment illustrates the tradeoff. Root-Gated obtains 77 optimality proofs against 73 for both comparators, with 43.00% less active worker occupancy than unconditional racing. These outcomes do not, however, establish the causal value of root dual degeneracy: several discordant proofs occur without gate activation. The historical analysis motivates the decision rule, while its predictive advantage requires further prospective validation.

The controller leaves SCIP’s source code and the original search trajectory unchanged. Its practical value nevertheless depends on the computing environment: root observations and process launches incur overhead, and savings in active worker occupancy free capacity only when the scheduler can reallocate idle cores. Repeated seed blocks, a prospective random gate, and reservation-aware scheduling would help distinguish the information value of the root statistic from execution variability.

7 Conclusion

Independent-seed replication exploits MIP performance variability but commits substantial computational resources. We developed a finite-deadline analysis of delayed replication and imperfect allocation decisions, examined replication opportunities across 101,615 seeded SCIP runs, and implemented a solver-external root-gated controller that preserves the original search trajectory.

In a prospective two-hour evaluation on 130 paired instances, Root-Gated proves optimality on 77 instances, compared with 73 for both single-seed solving and unconditional four-seed racing, while reducing active worker occupancy by 43.00% relative to unconditional racing. Although these results do not isolate the causal value of the root statistic, they demonstrate the feasibility of selective replication under a finite computational budget.

The broader insight is that solver variability is not only a phenomenon to measure or mitigate, but also an opportunity to allocate computational resources more intelligently.

0.A.1 Proof of Proposition 1

For a nonnegative random variable VV, the conditional survival-function identity gives

𝔼⁡[min⁡{V,b}∣ℐ]=∫0bPr⁡(V>t∣ℐ)​𝑑t.\mathbb{E}[\min\{V,b\}\mid\mathcal{I}]=\int_{0}^{b}\Pr(V>t\mid\mathcal{I})\,dt. (23)

Applying this identity to W0W_{0} and W1W_{1} yields

𝔼⁡[W0∣ℐ]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[W_{0}\mid\mathcal{I}] =∫0bS0​(t)​dt,\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{b}S_{0}(t)\,dt, (24)
𝔼⁡[W1∣ℐ]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[W_{1}\mid\mathcal{I}] =∫0bS1​(t)​dt.\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{b}S_{1}(t)\,dt.

Since S1​(t)=S0​(t)S_{1}(t)=S_{0}(t) for t<ht<h,

𝔼[W1−W0∣ℐ]=−∫hb[S0(t)−S1(t)]dt.\mathbb{E}[W_{1}-W_{0}\mid\mathcal{I}]=-\int_{h}^{b}[S_{0}(t)-S_{1}(t)]\,dt. (25)

The additional replicas consume processor time for (W1−h)+(W_{1}-h)_{+}. Because 0≤W1≤b0\leq W_{1}\leq b,

𝔼⁡[(W1−h)+∣ℐ]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(W_{1}-h)_{+}\mid\mathcal{I}] =∫hbPr⁡(W1>t∣ℐ)​𝑑t\displaystyle=\int_{h}^{b}\Pr(W_{1}>t\mid\mathcal{I})\,dt (26)
=∫hbS1​(t)​dt.\displaystyle=\int_{h}^{b}S_{1}(t)\,dt.

The difference in deadline-failure indicators is

𝟏{R>b,h+Y>b}−𝟏{R>b}\displaystyle\mathbf{1}_{\{R>b,\ h+Y>b\}}-\mathbf{1}_{\{R>b\}} (27)
=−𝟏{R>b,h+Y≤b}.\displaystyle=-\mathbf{1}_{\{R>b,\ h+Y\leq b\}}.

Furthermore,

Pr(R>b,h+Y≤b∣ℐ)\displaystyle\Pr(R>b,\ h+Y\leq b\mid\mathcal{I}) (28)
=Pr(R>b∣ℐ)−Pr(R>b,h+Y>b∣ℐ)\displaystyle=\Pr(R>b\mid\mathcal{I})-\Pr(R>b,\ h+Y>b\mid\mathcal{I})
=S0​(b)−S1​(b).\displaystyle=S_{0}(b)-S_{1}(b).

Substituting (25), (26), and (28) into the definition of Δ\Delta in (7), and taking conditional expectations, proves (8). □\square

0.A.2 Proof of Proposition 2

Because GG and G⋆G^{\star} are ℐ\mathcal{I}-measurable, the tower property gives

𝔼⁡[JG−JG⋆]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[J_{G}-J_{G^{\star}}] (29)
=𝔼⁡[(G−G⋆)​Δ]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[(G-G^{\star})\Delta]
=𝔼⁡[(G−G⋆)​𝔼​[Δ∣ℐ]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[(G-G^{\star})\mathbb{E}[\Delta\mid\mathcal{I}]]
=𝔼⁡[(G−G⋆)​δ​(ℐ)].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[(G-G^{\star})\delta(\mathcal{I})].

If δ⁡(ℐ)<0\delta(\mathcal{I})<0, then G⋆=1G^{\star}=1 and

(G−G⋆)δ(ℐ)=|δ(ℐ)|𝟏{G≠G⋆}.(G-G^{\star})\delta(\mathcal{I})=|\delta(\mathcal{I})|\mathbf{1}_{\{G\neq G^{\star}\}}. (30)

If δ⁡(ℐ)≥0\delta(\mathcal{I})\geq 0, then G⋆=0G^{\star}=0 and the same identity holds. In particular, when δ⁡(ℐ)=0\delta(\mathcal{I})=0, both sides vanish.

(G−G⋆)δ(ℐ)=|δ(ℐ)|𝟏{G≠G⋆}.(G-G^{\star})\delta(\mathcal{I})=|\delta(\mathcal{I})|\mathbf{1}_{\{G\neq G^{\star}\}}. (31)

0.A.3 Derivation of the Two-Replica Gini Identity

For independent copies X1X_{1} and X2X_{2} of a nonnegative random variable with 0<μ=𝔼⁡[X]<∞0<\mu=\mathbb{E}[X]<\infty,

min⁡{X1,X2}=X1+X2−|X1−X2|2.\min\{X_{1},X_{2}\}=\frac{X_{1}+X_{2}-|X_{1}-X_{2}|}{2}. (32)

Taking expectations,

𝔼⁡[M2]=μ−12​𝔼​|X1−X2|.\mathbb{E}[M_{2}]=\mu-\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}|X_{1}-X_{2}|. (33)

By the definition

GX=𝔼​|X1−X2|2​μ,G_{X}=\frac{\mathbb{E}|X_{1}-X_{2}|}{2\mu},

we obtain

𝔼⁡[M2]=μ⁡(1−GX).\mathbb{E}[M_{2}]=\mu(1-G_{X}). (34)

Under simultaneous execution, the two replicas consume aggregate processor time C2∞=2​M2C_{2}^{\infty}=2M_{2}. Consequently,

𝔼⁡[C2∞]=2​μ​(1−GX).\mathbb{E}[C_{2}^{\infty}]=2\mu(1-G_{X}). (35)

Since μ>0\mu>0,

𝔼[C2∞]<μ⟺GX>12.\mathbb{E}[C_{2}^{\infty}]<\mu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G_{X}>\frac{1}{2}. (36)

The same derivation applies to XT=min⁡{X,T}X^{T}=\min\{X,T\} for a finite deadline TT, provided its mean is positive. □\square
